stem: A 62-year-old woman with hypothyroidism has taken the same levothyroxine dose every morning for 5 years with a normal TSH. Two months ago calcium carbonate was started for osteoporosis, and she now takes both tablets together at breakfast. She has fatigue and constipation. The neck examination is unremarkable. TSH is raised and free T4 is low-normal.
oneliner: 62F + hypothyroidism stable on levothyroxine for 5 years + calcium carbonate started 2 months ago, taken together at breakfast + fatigue and constipation + raised TSH, low-normal free T4 + normal neck exam → best next step?
ask: Which of the following is the best next step?

options.A: Separate the two tablets by 4 hours and recheck TSH in 6 weeks
options.B: Stop the calcium carbonate permanently and recheck TSH
options.C: Replace levothyroxine with liothyronine at a matching dose
options.D: Measure anti-thyroid peroxidase antibodies before any change
options.E: Order a thyroid ultrasound to look for a nodule

whyNot.B: She **needs the calcium for osteoporosis**; spacing the tablets solves the problem without stopping it
whyNot.C: She was **stable for 5 years** on levothyroxine; the change began only with the **calcium**
whyNot.D: Hypothyroidism is already **established and was controlled for 5 years**, so the cause is not in question
whyNot.E: The **neck examination is unremarkable**, and a nodule would not explain a TSH rise that began with the calcium

answer: Separate the two tablets by 4 hours and recheck TSH in 6 weeks
why: A **stable levothyroxine dose** and a **rising TSH after calcium carbonate was started** (taken together) means the calcium is binding the thyroid hormone in the gut and lowering absorption. Take levothyroxine **on an empty stomach, about 4 hours apart from calcium**, then recheck TSH in about 6 weeks.

idea.rule: Anything that binds levothyroxine in the gut or impairs its absorption lowers its effect, so give it alone on an empty stomach.
also: Iron and antacids containing aluminum or magnesium
Proton pump inhibitors, by raising gastric pH
Coffee, soy and high-fiber meals taken with the tablet

stem: A 76-year-old man with diabetes and hypertension has had exertional chest tightness, relieved by rest, for a year. He now reports 6 months of cold intolerance, constipation and dry skin. He is alert, his temperature is normal and his pulse is 54/min. TSH is 48 mU/L and free T4 is low.
oneliner: 76M + diabetes + hypertension + exertional angina + cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin + alert, normal temperature + TSH 48 + low free T4 → how to start treatment?
ask: Which is the most appropriate way to start thyroid hormone replacement?

options.A: A full weight-based dose of levothyroxine from the first day
options.B: A low dose of levothyroxine, raised slowly over weeks
options.D: No treatment until the angina has been treated surgically

whyNot.A: His **age and exertional angina** make a sudden rise in cardiac demand dangerous
whyNot.C: Acts fast and briefly, raising heart rate and demand; risky with his **exertional angina**
whyNot.D: His symptoms come from **severe hypothyroidism (TSH 48)**; treatment can start cautiously now
whyNot.E: Reserved for severe decompensation; he is **alert with a normal temperature**

answer: A low dose of levothyroxine, raised slowly over weeks
why: **Primary hypothyroidism** (high TSH, low free T4) in a **76-year-old with exertional angina** calls for a **low starting dose of levothyroxine** with slow titration. Restoring thyroid hormone raises heart rate and oxygen demand, which can precipitate angina or arrhythmia.

idea.rule: Thyroid hormone raises cardiac demand, so start low and go slow when the heart is at risk.

stem: A 51-year-old man with rheumatoid arthritis took prednisone 10 mg every day for 9 months. When his tablets ran out last week he did not refill them. He now has fatigue, weakness, joint pain, nausea and dizziness on standing, and his blood pressure is 86/54 mm Hg. His morning cortisol and ACTH are both low.
oneliner: 51M + rheumatoid arthritis + prednisone 10 mg daily for 9 months + stopped abruptly last week + fatigue, weakness, nausea, orthostatic dizziness + BP 86/54 + low cortisol and low ACTH → what would have prevented this?
ask: Which measure would most likely have prevented this?

options.A: Stopping the prednisone abruptly as soon as the joint disease was controlled
options.B: Adding fludrocortisone alone for the duration of treatment
options.C: Switching to an equal-strength dose of dexamethasone
options.D: Changing to an NSAID and stopping the steroid without tapering
options.E: Reducing the dose gradually, with extra steroid during illness or surgery

whyNot.A: That is **what happened**: abrupt withdrawal after **9 months of daily prednisone** caused his crisis
whyNot.B: A mineralocorticoid does not replace the missing **cortisol**; the suppressed axis shows as **low ACTH and cortisol**
whyNot.C: Any glucocorticoid at this strength for **9 months** suppresses ACTH; long-acting dexamethasone suppresses it even more
whyNot.D: Still **stops the steroid abruptly** after 9 months, so the same crisis would follow

answer: Reducing the dose gradually, with extra steroid during illness or surgery
why: **Months of daily prednisone** suppress the HPA axis, so **ACTH and cortisol are low** and the adrenal cortex shrinks. Stopping abruptly leaves him unable to make cortisol, causing weakness and hypotension. Prevention is a **gradual taper** and **stress-dose steroid** during illness or surgery.

idea.rule: Exogenous glucocorticoid suppresses ACTH; the adrenals recover slowly, so withdraw gradually.
also: Suppression is expected after about 3 weeks or more of daily supraphysiologic doses
Stress doses are needed during surgery, infection or trauma
Secondary adrenal insufficiency: low ACTH and cortisol, normal aldosterone
The zona glomerulosa is spared, so hyperkalemia is not expected
